cards.title: Use Volume Quotes to Reset Your Unit Cost Baseline
cards.summary: Post RFQs at multiple volume tiers to find how far per-unit cost falls, then weigh the discount against cash flow and defect risk.
cards.use_when: Product selection or replenishment: you are reordering a proven SKU and want to know whether moving from small Aliexpress-style batches to a bulk Alibaba order is worth the capital lock-up.
steps: Confirm the SKU already sells at a healthy margin before scaling. The source's jewellery example sold at $7.80 cost / $25.99 retail from weekly 500-unit batches.

Post several Request For Quotation (RFQ) listings on Alibaba for the same product rather than accepting the first quote, because the same item appeared anywhere from $10 down to $4.00 depending on order size.

Ask each supplier to quote explicitly at your target volume (the source cites ~10K units landing near $2.00 per unit versus $7.80 in small batches) plus one tier below and one above, so you see the slope of the discount.

Compare the discount against the cash required and the storage risk of holding that inventory; a deep unit-cost cut is not automatically the better decision if it ties up working capital you need elsewhere.
Treat all figures as example quotes from one jewellery case, not benchmarks — your category, material and current market will differ.
caveats: Volume discounts are the source author's experience with jewellery, not a general pricing guarantee.

A commenter with sourcing/manufacturing background notes that unused volume or freight-consolidation discounts can be more valuable leveraged in other ways (e.g. cash-flow structures) than taken as a straight price cut.

cards.title: Size defect allowances from observed quality instead of a fixed surplus
cards.summary: Use sample and batch defect evidence to plan usable stock while preventing defects through specifications and inspection.
cards.use_when: Purchase-order planning: you are placing or replenishing a bulk order and deciding the exact quantity to commit to.
steps: Assume a fraction of any bulk shipment will arrive broken or sub-quality. The source ordered 10K units and received roughly 300 defective pieces.
Use measured reject rates to estimate usable units; the source's 10% extra-order recommendation is not a standard. A defect allowance does not replace agreed quality criteria or corrective action.
Decide whether to inspect yourself or pay a third-party inspector, which the source cites at roughly $200 per inspection, when the order value makes self-inspection impractical.
Weigh whether to ship defects back to the supplier. In the source's case the supplier asked for returns but the author judged the time cost not worth it, so the buffer absorbed the loss instead.
Settle quality-check responsibility before shipping to customers: unlike Amazon, Alibaba does not inspect on your behalf.
caveats: The 10% figure and the 300-defect count come from one 10K-unit jewellery order and are illustrative, not a universal defect rate.
The $200 inspector cost is a cited example price and will vary by market and inspection scope.

cards.title: Test New Suppliers With Small Batches Before Switching
cards.summary: Run a cheaper supplier through a small test order while keeping your incumbent, and only migrate after verifying quality.
cards.use_when: Supplier negotiation or cost reduction: you've found a vendor quoting materially less and are tempted to move your whole order.
steps: Keep your current supplier active. The source explicitly warns against ditching a supplier too early.
Place a limited test order with the cheaper supplier — the author's example was 500 units against a cost that was ~20% lower than the incumbent.
Inspect the test batch before committing volume. In the source's case most of the 500 units were defective, which would have been catastrophic at full order size.
Maintain multiple qualified vendors so you always have a fallback if one fails inspection or raises prices.
Only migrate your supply chain once the new supplier has proven defect rates comparable to your incumbent; until then, treat the cheaper quote as a hypothesis, not a saving.
caveats: This is a risk-management heuristic from one bad experience, not a guarantee that cheap suppliers fail.
A test batch adds cost and lead time; factor that into the decision.

cards.title: Document order terms and pay through the protected Alibaba order route
cards.summary: Route supplier payments through Alibaba's built-in gateway for buyer protection rather than direct transfers.
cards.use_when: Supplier payment: you are about to send a deposit or balance to a Chinese supplier and choosing the payment method.
steps: Record product specifications, agreed quality, quantity and shipment terms in the Trade Assurance order.
Pay through Alibaba's authorized checkout or official bank details for that order. A wire transfer through Alibaba differs from paying a supplier directly off-platform.
Keep specifications, communications, samples and inspection evidence for a potential dispute.
Verify current order eligibility, coverage and claim deadlines before payment. The source commenter's off-platform discount proposal sacrifices platform protection and is not a substitute for it.
caveats: Protection depends on the order and applicable terms; it does not replace supplier vetting or quality inspection.

cards.title: Get a Direct Messaging Channel to Avoid Supplier Ghosting
cards.summary: Collect the supplier's WhatsApp, WeChat or email early so an offline Alibaba chat thread doesn't stall your order.
cards.use_when: Supplier communication during quoting, sampling, production or shipping: you need reliable contact to confirm specs, defects or shipment timing.
steps: When you first make contact through Alibaba chat, immediately request the salesperson's email plus WhatsApp, WeChat or whatever messaging app they use.
Treat the native Alibaba chat as unreliable for time-sensitive matters: the source says suppliers will go offline without prior notice.
Keep the direct channel for anything that affects a shipping deadline or defect claim — for example, confirming FedEx tracking or flagging a defective batch before a reorder.
Confirm key terms in writing on the direct channel as well, so you have a record if the sale rep changes or the Alibaba thread is abandoned.
caveats: The source does not specify what to do if a supplier refuses to share direct contact details; that may itself be a diligence signal.

cards.title: Match Shipping Method to Item Weight and Deadline
cards.summary: Choose sea freight, air cargo, or premium courier based on item weight and how far ahead of peak season you order.
cards.use_when: Fulfillment planning and replenishment timing: you are ordering heavy or bulky products and deciding how they get to your warehouse.
steps: Check unit weight before committing to a product. The source's kitchen-product example weighed 1.2 kg and was stainless steel — too heavy for cheap fast shipping.

Compare landed timing: sea containers were the affordable option but carried a roughly one-month transit; air cargo was fast but quoted at ~$2,000 for that order, which the author considered expensive when Q4 was already close.
Order heavy items well ahead of your selling season so you can use sea freight instead of paying a rush premium.

For large orders where you have a good supplier relationship, ask for premium courier (FedEx/UPS) instead of ePacket. The source's supplier upgraded large orders to FedEx, cutting California delivery from 10–14 days to 4–5 days.
Note the context: the source author cites ePacket's decline after 2019/COVID, so verify current carrier options rather than designing around ePacket.
caveats: The $2,000 air quote, one-month sea transit and 4–5 day FedEx times are examples from a specific order and route, not fixed rates.
Premium courier availability depends on order size and relationship, not a standard entitlement.

cards.title: Negotiate Down Per-Unit Cost Before You Commit Volume
cards.summary: Ask suppliers for a lower unit price rather than accepting the initial quote; small per-unit reductions compound across a large order.
cards.use_when: Supplier negotiation: you have a quote in hand for a replenishment or new-product bulk order and are deciding whether to push back on price.
steps: Treat the first quote as an opening position, not a final price. The source got a per-product cost from $6 down to $4.80 through direct negotiation.
Quantify the saving before you decide how hard to push: the author notes that $1.20 reduction saved roughly $3,500 per order at his volume, which is why the effort was worth it.

Negotiate alongside volume, payment and shipping terms rather than price alone — suppliers may offer freight consolidation or other concessions instead of a price cut if cash flow constrains your order size.

A commenter with sourcing expertise suggests unused discounts (volume, consolidated freight) can be repurposed creatively — for example, funding a larger order to unlock a lower tier and structuring payments around it — so ask what other levers exist beyond the sticker price.
Do not present a source's negotiated outcome as your expected result; your leverage depends on volume, category and supplier.
caveats: The $6→$4.80 and $3,500 figures are from the author's own order and are examples, not benchmarks.
Aggressive negotiation can damage a relationship, so weigh it against long-term supply reliability.

cards.title: Use Sourcing Agents Deliberately and Vet Them
cards.summary: Sourcing agents can unlock manufacturer access, customisation and better pricing, but require diligence on who you choose.
cards.use_when: Product selection and sourcing strategy: you need customisation, factory-direct access, or better prices than trading-company quotes on Alibaba.
steps: Consider a sourcing agent when you need to reach the actual manufacturer rather than a reseller, when you want customisation applied to a product, or when quoted prices on Alibaba appear inflated.
Expect the agent to negotiate directly with the manufacturer on your behalf and potentially unlock better unit economics than you can get alone.
Vet the agent carefully. The source author states plainly that agents can be great but warns to use a better one, without giving specific selection criteria.

Because the source does not define selection criteria, apply your own diligence: verify references, sample their work on a small order, and confirm they disclose the manufacturer relationship before you commit volume.
Do not treat agent savings as guaranteed; the source only asserts potential for better prices and customisation.
caveats: The source offers no concrete vetting checklist or red flags for agents — only a general warning.
An agent adds a margin layer, so confirm the net landed cost is actually lower after their fee.
cards.source_name: What I learnt from sourcing e-commerce products from China.docx

cards.title: Structure Bulk Purchases Around Cash Flow, Not Just Unit Price
cards.summary: Unused volume and freight discounts can be leveraged through payment or inventory structures rather than taken as straight price cuts.
cards.use_when: Replenishment and cash-flow planning: you are ordering a recurring SKU several times a year and weighing a larger order tier against working capital.
steps: The source describes a 30% deposit and 70% pre-shipment balance as one structure; confirm actual milestones and contractual terms for your order.

Note the commenter's scenario: a client re-ordering the same product multiple times a year at roughly $10 landed cost. An outside party adds capital to increase the order to a full year's supply, unlocking a volume discount while keeping the client's per-unit cost unchanged at $10.
The client receives the full year of stock, and only pays the outside party as they consume inventory — removing lead time and MOQ on the portion already warehoused, and improving cash flow.

For an ecommerce operator, this suggests a decision: if a volume tier would strain cash flow, look for investors or distributors willing to fund the gap and be repaid as you sell through, rather than declining the discount entirely.
This is a commenter's specific client arrangement, not a standard market practice; structure any such deal with clear inventory ownership and repayment terms.
caveats: This is one commenter's model, not a proven universal method.
Splitting inventory ownership introduces legal and accounting complexity that the source does not address.
